name: visit-preparation

# Visit Preparation

Prepare upcoming encounters so the physician enters each visit oriented to the patient's course,
recent clinical changes, open work, and the decisions the visit can settle.

## Selecting Visits and Timing

Judge each upcoming appointment on its clinical context, lead time, and available patient evidence
rather than applying a fixed rule to every slot:

- Prepare now when a visit is imminent or in progress, or when hospital discharge records, critical
  interval results, unstable symptoms, or complex medication transitions are already in hand and
  benefit from immediate synthesis.
- Schedule preparation closer to the visit when an appointment is days away and pending laboratory
  panels, imaging reports, specialist notes, or home monitoring updates may still arrive, leaving
  enough lead time for pre-visit review.
- Defer and check again when key expected records have not yet arrived and the visit is still well
  ahead.
- Skip preparation only when a visit genuinely needs no pre-visit chart synthesis (such as a pure
  administrative or immunization-only slot with an unremarkable, stable chart), and state the
  patient-specific reason. Never start preparation after a visit has ended.

Ground every selection reason in the appointment's purpose, timing, and the patient's chart
evidence, open concerns, and source freshness.

## Authoring a Visit Briefing

Before saving a briefing, review saved patient understanding, active patient memory, and relevant
prior workspace work, refresh stale connected sources when newer records could alter the visit
plan, and open exact chart revisions to verify dated facts. When guideline or drug-labeling detail
sharpens a visit option, verify it in the clinical library using clinical concepts only, never
patient identifiers.

Structure the briefing around four clinical duties:

1. Trajectory: how the patient's principal conditions, symptoms, and physiological markers have
   moved over time, with dates and direction rather than isolated snapshots.
2. Meaningful interval changes: new laboratory or imaging results, medication changes, outside
   emergency or hospital care, specialist recommendations, and patient-shared updates since the
   prior encounter.
3. Unresolved follow-up: pending studies, unclosed referrals, monitoring overdue from earlier
   plans, discrepant medication lists, or unanswered patient questions.
4. Visit decisions: concrete clinical questions and management options the upcoming visit can
   settle. Present every recommendation strictly as an option or question for the physician to
   consider, never as an accepted order, completed medication change, or settled plan.

Keep consequential uncertainty right beside the conclusion it qualifies rather than burying all
caveats at the bottom. When accounts conflict, a key outside note is missing, an attachment is
unreadable, or a source refresh failed, adjust clinical confidence accordingly, work from the
available verified records, and state the exact freshness and limits in the basis and limitations
summary.

Write the schedule-card orientation as a concise one-to-two sentence summary that agrees with the
briefing's central clinical picture and key visit focus.

## Raising a Pre-Visit Concern

Most prepared visits need only their saved briefing. Raise a pre-visit concern only when
preparation uncovers actionable clinical news the physician should see before walking into the
visit:

- Use urgent (`now`) priority when a finding demands immediate physician attention before the
  visit (such as a dangerously abnormal laboratory value, acute decompensation, or critical safety
  conflict).
- Use same-day (`today`) priority when pre-visit awareness materially changes preparation before
  the encounter (such as an unexpected recent hospitalization, important new specialist change, or
  pre-visit action needed ahead of the slot).
- Omit a pre-visit concern for routine interval follow-up that can wait until the physician opens
  the briefing for the visit.
